title: AI analytics agents compared: what each one can see
summary: Six AI analytics tools compared by the evidence they read, how they work, and where they stop, for teams asking why GA4 and ad conversions dropped.
body_markdown:
**Last reviewed: October 15, 2026.** Features and pricing change quickly. Treat this page as a buying map, not a scorecard, and check each vendor’s own pages before you sign.


If you want an AI that can look at GA4 and your ad campaigns and explain why conversions dropped, the deciding question is where the tool gets its evidence. Some tools reason over the numbers that platforms and stores report. Some answer questions over data that already reached a warehouse or a semantic model. A third kind reads the data as it is produced, before any report, which is the only place a broken tag and a weaker campaign look different.


No tool does every job. A warehouse agent can explain data that arrived; it can’t show that a pixel double-fired after a GTM release, or that a purchase lost its value before the hit was sent. And an agent that works at the source doesn’t replace a governed warehouse model for financial reporting or broad business intelligence.


## Start with the evidence layer


“AI analytics” covers several kinds of product. Three matter for a conversion-drop question:


1. **AI for ads, marketing, and performance.** These tools join channel, attribution, site, and revenue numbers to decide where to spend and what to change.
2. **AI for business intelligence.** These tools answer natural-language questions against governed models in Snowflake, BigQuery, or a semantic layer.
3. **Agents that work at the source.** These read the data as it is produced — the hit, the` dataLayer` , the pixel, the CAPI payload, the consent state, the GTM release — and check whether a reported change is real or a measurement break.


Marketing pipelines (Funnel, Supermetrics) and downstream data-quality tools sit next to these, but they move or test data after collection rather than explain a drop. The categories can work together. They are not interchangeable.


## Quick comparison


Tool Category What it reads How it works Where it stops Pricing model


GoMarble AI for ads and performance GA4, Search Console, ad platforms, Shopify, Klaviyo, BigQuery, and Snowflake through AI workflows Investigations and trend analysis in a connected AI client Compares recorded outcomes across systems; its page doesn’t describe request-level evidence Free plan; paid plans by tier


Triple Whale AI for ads and performance Ecommerce, attribution, and channel data through its own data platform and pixel Agents for analysis and anomalies; on higher plans, scheduled checks and actions within guardrails Ecommerce-first; doesn’t position itself on consent, tags, or payloads Free tier; paid plans by GMV and package


Northbeam AI for ads and performance First-party marketing and conversion data Attribution and forecasting models Its AI page covers modeling, not event-level debugging Published tiers plus custom


ThoughtSpot Spotter AI for business intelligence Live warehouse data through a semantic layer Follow-up analysis, change analysis, and forecasting Needs governed models; doesn’t claim to inspect the browser or pixel payload Per user, plus custom Enterprise


Looker AI for business intelligence Data modeled in LookML and connected cloud sources Conversational analytics and dashboard agents on a semantic layer Relies on the model and downstream data, not the original request Platform by quote


[Trackingplan](https://www.trackingplan.com/) Agent at the source Hits,` dataLayer` , consent state, and GTM releases across 170+ analytics and ad providers; spend, impressions, clicks, and conversions per campaign from eleven ad networks Always-on monitoring against a learned baseline, plus an agent you ask in the app, in Slack, or through MCP in Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor Not a warehouse BI suite or an attribution model; tag manager history covers GTM only Sessions plus credits: Starter 89€, Growth 699€, Enterprise 2,000€ per month


The table compares published product positioning, not independent tests. “How it works” uses each vendor’s own description, and words like “agent” or “proactive” don’t mean the same thing across products.


## GoMarble connects reporting systems


GoMarble’s marketing analytics workflows connect an AI client to GA4, Search Console, ad platforms, Shopify, Klaviyo, BigQuery, and Snowflake. Its example for a conversion-rate drop checks traffic mix, channel composition, on-site behavior, and store orders.


Choose it when the question crosses several reporting systems: did traffic mix or on-site behavior move the rate, do paid visitors turn into store revenue, does recorded conversion volume disagree with orders?


Its evidence is the recorded outcome in each system. That is useful, but it isn’t the original request, consent state,` dataLayer` , or tag trigger. When the answer has to name the implementation change behind a break, it needs a source-level layer.


## Triple Whale runs ecommerce operations


Triple Whale describes agents for acquisition, conversion, retention, and operations, including order and revenue pacing and revenue anomalies. They run on top of its own measurement platform and pixel; on its higher plans they can also schedule checks and reports and act across ad accounts within approval settings and guardrails.


Choose it when the central problem is ecommerce growth: which products, creatives, or channels drive profitable revenue, and which recurring work can be automated.


Its scope is a commerce data platform, attribution, and execution. It doesn’t present itself as a monitor of consent states, GTM triggers, or outgoing payloads, so it consumes conversion data rather than validating how that data was produced.


## Northbeam models attribution and spend


Northbeam describes machine-learning models that use first-party data to attribute conversions across the buyer journey and forecast performance at different spend levels, with product-level views of CAC, ROAS, and spend.


Choose it when the decision is about media efficiency and budget allocation.


Its published material describes modeling and forecasting, not request-level inspection of pixels, parameters, consent, or releases. When the model shows a sudden drop, you still need to know whether demand changed or a conversion signal broke.


## ThoughtSpot Spotter answers on governed data


ThoughtSpot describes Spotter as an AI analyst that turns questions into governed SQL on a semantic layer, supports follow-up analysis, enforces row- and column-level security, and shows the steps behind an answer.


Choose it when business users need self-serve answers on modeled data with consistent metric definitions.


Spotter is bounded by the warehouse and model it queries. It can explain a modeled conversion decline; it doesn’t position itself as a monitor of the browser request,` dataLayer` , consent event, or pixel payload that produced the record.


## Looker governs the semantic layer


Google Cloud positions Looker as agentic BI on a semantic layer, with conversational analytics, dashboard agents, MCP integration, and LookML to give people and agents one definition of each metric.


Choose it when the priority is governed business intelligence: metrics defined once and reused across dashboards and agents.


Like every semantic layer, it governs the data it receives. A clean LookML definition can’t repair a pixel that stopped firing.


## Trackingplan sees the data behind the numbers


Trackingplan fits when the question is not only “what changed?” but “did the system send the right data in the first place?” Claude or ChatGPT connected to your analytics tool sees the numbers it reports. Trackingplan’s agent sees the data behind them. That is what the[AI analytics agent](https://www.trackingplan.com/landings/ai-analytics-agent) is built for.


[Coverage](https://www.trackingplan.com/landings/coverage) captures every outgoing request where it is produced and parses each payload per platform: events, values, IDs, and consent flags. Since October, the agent also reads spend, impressions, clicks, and conversions per campaign from Google Ads, Meta Ads, LinkedIn Ads, TikTok Ads, Snapchat Ads, Pinterest Ads, Microsoft Ads, X Ads, Amazon Ads, Apple Search Ads, and Reddit Ads, so traffic and spend sit in the same answer.


That makes a different kind of diagnosis possible:


- A conversion drop is checked against a missing event, a broken pixel, a duplicate fire, or a changed payload.
- A platform discrepancy is traced to a different value, currency, click ID, or deduplication key.
- A consent problem is located per hit, vendor, and market, not inferred from a report.
- A release regression is tied to the GTM change that caused it.


The agent names a cause only when two independent pieces of evidence agree; otherwise it labels the answer a hypothesis, and every answer shows the queries behind it. How that discipline is built into the[agent harness](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/agent-harness-for-marketing-data) is a story of its own. The[paid media](https://www.trackingplan.com/landings/paid-media) page shows the workflow: Pixel vs CAPI vs GA4, the same purchase counted once, with gaps quantified before bidding acts on them.


The limit matters as much. Trackingplan doesn’t replace a warehouse semantic model, a BI platform, or a multi-touch attribution model. It makes the data feeding them inspectable.


## Match the first question to the tool


If the first question is… Start with… Why


“Did traffic mix, on-site behavior, or revenue cause the decline?” GoMarble It connects GA4, ads, search, and commerce reports.


“Which channels, products, or touchpoints deserve more budget?” Triple Whale or Northbeam They focus on ecommerce operations, attribution, and forecasting.


“Can the business answer warehouse questions consistently?” ThoughtSpot or Looker They answer over governed models and data platforms.


“Conversions dropped in GA4 and in the ad platforms. Is it the campaign or the tracking?”[Trackingplan’s AI analytics agent](https://www.trackingplan.com/landings/ai-analytics-agent) It reads the hits where they are produced, plus campaign spend, clicks, and conversions, in the same answer.


The strongest stack isn’t the one with the most autonomous language. It is the one that can show the evidence path from the hit, to the recorded event, to the modeled metric, to the decision.


## Pricing isn’t directly comparable


The tools charge for different things, so a “cheapest tool” ranking would mislead:


- ThoughtSpot charges per user, with a custom Enterprise tier.
- Triple Whale has a free tier and prices paid plans by GMV and package.
- GoMarble has a free plan and paid plans by tier.
- Northbeam publishes some tiers and quotes the rest.
- Looker’s platform is priced by quote.
- Trackingplan charges by sessions plus agent credits: Starter 89€, Growth 699€, and Enterprise 2,000€ per month, on the[pricing page](https://www.trackingplan.com/pricing) .


Compare total cost, not the subscription line: source connections, warehouse compute, modeling work, attribution methodology, implementation upkeep, credits, ad-account actions, and the analyst time needed to check every answer.


## Questions to ask every vendor


Ask each one to work through the same incident with the same evidence:


1. A conversion rate drops after a release. What does the tool inspect first?
2. Can it tell a demand change from a missing or duplicate event?
3. Can it show the original payload, the affected parameter, the consent state, and the destination?
4. Can it compare browser, server-side, and platform-reported conversions?
5. What happens when a source is delayed, incomplete, or wrong?
6. Can a person review the evidence and correct the explanation?
7. Which actions are recommendations, which are automated, and which need approval?
8. How are definitions, assumptions, permissions, and decisions recorded?
9. What doesn’t the tool see?
10. How do sessions, seats, queries, credits, compute, and media spend affect the price?
